articles.title: Computational approaches to deep learning–driven EEG analysis for neurological disease diagnosis: a systematic review
articles.content: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a widely used non-invasive neurophysiological technique for analyzing brain dynamics and diagnosing neurological diseases. However, the non-stationary nature, low signal-to-noise ratio, and inter-subject variability of EEG signals cause significant challenges to traditional analytical approaches. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful computational tool for EEG analysis, which enables automated feature learning and improved diagnostic accuracy with minimal human-driven feature extraction. This review systematically explains computational approaches in deep learning-driven EEG analysis for the diagnosis of neurological diseases. It includes recent advances in deep learning architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), hybrid configurations, Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Large Language Models (LLM), autoencoders, and transformer-based models, with a focus on their capacity to model spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal dynamics in EEG signals. This is applicable in diagnosing major neurological disorders such as Epilepsy, Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Encephalopathy, Parkinson’s disease (PD), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), sleep disorders, and developmental brain disorders. Furthermore, we discuss essential preprocessing strategies and denoising techniques, showing how removing biological artifacts prevents diagnostic models from confusing noise with actual signs of disease. Key challenges such as limited data availability, lack of model interpretability, inter-subject variability, and difficulty in clinical translation are identified and critically discussed. Finally, key emerging trends and future research directions are identified to support the development of clinical applications of EEG-based disease diagnostic systems.

articles.title: Exploratory evaluation of electroencephalogram-derived features for classification of mild cognitive impairment in two independent datasets
articles.content: A proper diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is one of the important challenges in the early detection of dementia. For the classification of MCI patients and healthy controls, some electroencephalogram (EEG)-derived indices were calculated and compared. Some studies have been conducted on the high accuracy classification of MCI patients and healthy controls, but classification may depend on the dataset and recording conditions. In this study, we evaluated EEG-derived indices in the Japanese and the Iranian EEG datasets and examined their classification performance under within-dataset and cross-dataset validation. This classifier had common features but was learned for each dataset. The Japanese dataset consisted of 7 MCI patients and 10 healthy controls. The Iranian dataset consisted of 29 MCI patients and 32 healthy controls. The common 16 EEG data were separated into 5 frequency bands. Power spectrum and SL values by Synchronization Likelihood were calculated as features for classification. These standardized and exponentially transformed indices were also used as features. Furthermore, graph metrics were calculated based on SL values before or after standardization and exponential transformation. Features used for classification were selected from these indices. The high classification accuracies were obtained from the classifier using a 34-dimensional feature subset selected from standardized and exponentially transformed EEG-derived indices for lower alpha band. Accuracies of this classifier were 88.24% in the Japanese dataset and 86.89% in the Iranian dataset. To evaluate classification accuracy while minimizing information leakage and optimistic bias, nested leave-one-out cross-validation was performed. Accuracies were 88.24% in the Japanese dataset and 83.61% in the Iranian dataset using exponentially transformed EEG-derived indices for lower alpha band. To evaluate whether the classifier can generalize to independent datasets obtained under different recording conditions, exploratory bidirectional cross-dataset evaluation was performed. Accuracies were 40.98% (Training data: the Japanese dataset, Test data: the Iranian dataset) and 58.82% (Training data: the Iranian dataset, Test data: the Japanese dataset). These findings suggested that resting-state EEG-derived indices for lower alpha band may contain information useful for classification of MCI patients and healthy controls. However, they suggested that classifier based on these indices may partly reflect dataset-specific characteristics.

articles.title: Short excitatory projections promote burst activity and modular functional organization in neural networks
articles.content: Physical constraints in the brain favor short, distance-dependent connections. However, short-range projections are not merely a structural compromise; they also serve essential functional roles. Here, we explore networks with balanced excitation and inhibition, demonstrating that short excitatory projections increase the number of common presynaptic inputs, thereby enhancing the correlations of neural responses. Strengthened recurrent correlations can lead to bursting states, amplifying postsynaptic neuronal activity and supporting signal propagation over long distances within the network. Moreover, even without an explicitly imposed modular structure, short excitatory connections can give rise to functional clustering and support a broad spectrum of modular functions. In this model, short excitatory projections are associated with the emergence of column-like functional organization and dynamic burst propagation from a single structural principle, offering a candidate mechanism by which the brain could transform structural wiring constraints into opportunities for complex computation and distributed processing. These findings motivate further work on how such structural limitations may more generally be turned into computational opportunities in biological circuits.
articles.author: Claus C. Hilgetag

articles.title: Persistent memory through triple-loop consolidation under stochastic unit turnover
articles.content: Dissipative cognitive architectures maintain computation through continuous energy expenditure, where units that exhaust their energy are stochastically replaced with fresh random state. This creates a fundamental challenge: how can persistent, context-specific memory survive when all learnable state is periodically destroyed? Existing memory mechanisms—including elastic weight consolidation, synaptic intelligence, and surprise-driven gating—rely on gradient computation and are inapplicable to dissipative systems that do not perform it. We introduce Deep Memory (DM), a backpropagation-free persistent memory mechanism operating through a triple-loop consolidation cycle: (1) recording of expert-specific content centroids during active computation, (2) seeding of replaced units with stored representations, and (3) stabilization through continuous re-entry that counteracts dissipative drift. We demonstrate that discrete expert routing via Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) gating is required, in the regimes tested, for DM functionality, preventing the centroid convergence that would render stored memories identical. Across 972 simulation runs spanning thirteen experimental blocks, we establish: (i) removing stable context–expert binding removes structural specialization (MI = 1.10 vs. 0.001 under binding destruction; n = 91); (ii) DM achieves persistent representation quality R = 0.984 compared to 0.385 without memory (n = 16); (iii) continuous seeding reconstructs representations after interference (Rrecon = 0.978; one-shot seeding fails; n = 30); (iv) the mechanism operates within a well-characterized (K, ρ) envelope with identifiable degradation boundaries (n = 350); (v) a factorial ablation isolates recording × seeding as the minimal critical dyad (n = 40); and (vi) six confirmatory experiments—including single-factor causal ablation, mediation analysis, and comparison with associative and reservoir baselines (Hopfield, ESN) under matched turnover—validate what the mechanism requires and how it compares with those baselines (n = 370). Results (ii)–(v) rest on pilot-scale seed counts (4–5 seeds per condition); at these counts no paired non-parametric test can reach p < 0.05 whatever the effect size, so we report them as estimates of effect size and direction rather than as confirmatory tests. Within these limits, DM is a falsifiable, bounded mechanism for persistent memory in backpropagation-free cognitive systems. Its relation to hippocampal consolidation is a functional analogy only: DM shares the premise of a store held apart from the computing substrate, but assigns the fast and slow roles in the opposite direction to complementary learning systems theory.
articles.author: Jianwei Lou

articles.title: Temporal dissociation across the eye-brain-muscle cascade delineates a preparation window before muscle activation in subacute stroke
articles.content: Upper-limb motor impairment after stroke is compounded by a disrupted sensorimotor cascade linking visual attention, cortical motor preparation, and peripheral muscle activation. Whether these stages are temporally dissociated in subacute stroke, and whether their timing carries information about the preparation and execution of a reaching action, remains unclear. Thirty subacute stroke survivors and 30 healthy controls performed a full-plane nine-grid reaching task while eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and surface electromyography (EMG) were recorded synchronously. Three neurophysiological latencies were extracted: first fixation on the target, stimulus-locked lateralized readiness potential (s-LRP) onset, and peripheral muscle activation onset. Compared with controls, patients showed a stepwise delay across the cascade, with delayed visual engagement (616.73 ms vs. 367.86 ms) and delayed peripheral muscle activation (1,080 ms vs. 605 ms) bracketing a cortical preparation window. A random-forest classifier was trained on window-level gaze-timing features, computed separately for each target-presentation and inter-target interval of the task. Under participant-level leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, it achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.973 (95% CI 0.958–0.984) and an accuracy of 0.918, numerically the highest among the five classifiers compared. These findings describe a quantifiable temporal organization of the sensorimotor cascade in the subacute stage of stroke and indicate that gaze timing carries discriminative information about the occurrence of an instructed reaching action. They establish a descriptive, testable framework rather than a demonstrated clinical benefit. Validation in chronic stroke and across independent samples is further required.
articles.author: Jing Tao

articles.title: Effectiveness of bimanual kinesthetic teaching through different controller settings
articles.content: Physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) through kinesthetic teaching enables intuitive robot programming, but extending this approach to bimanual systems introduces challenges in synchronized control. Thus, the best way to control bimanual robot systems for kinesthetic teaching remains unclear. In this paper we evaluate bimanual kinesthetic teaching from the demonstrator's perspective, showing how different modes of control can affect both demonstration performance and user experience. Our study, in which participants kinesthetically taught a bimanual robot to perform a pick-and-place task, showed that the relative stiffness of the two robots significantly affects task timing and operator perception.
articles.author: Andrej Gams

articles.title: From beat to syntax: evolutionary and developmental paths of a shared neural resource for hierarchical processing in music and language
articles.content: Children who track a musical beat well tend to have stronger grammatical skills, and brief exposure to a regular rhythm can transiently improve grammatical processing. These findings raise the possibility of a shared underlying mechanism, and with it two questions: where did the link come from, and when does it emerge in development? Our central hypothesis is that beat perception, the extraction and prediction of a metrical pulse, and hierarchical syntactic structure building draw on a common computational principle, predictive neural entrainment: the alignment of cortical activity to rhythmic input in a way that enables temporal anticipation. Comparative work indicates that non-human primates track regular input but show little evidence of beat-based prediction. We propose that during hominin evolution the expanding prefrontal cortex exerted stronger top-down control over the auditory-motor pathway, extending an ancestral timing system to meet the hierarchical demands of syntax. For development, we distinguish capacities present in infancy, including beat sensitivity and temporal prediction, from the later coupling of beat-based prediction to syntax, which we hypothesize depends on fronto-temporal maturation; when that coupling emerges is an empirical question. We integrate neuroimaging, comparative, developmental, and clinical evidence into a three-layer model: temporal encoding, structural grouping, and hierarchical prediction, each tied to a distinct neural signature. The model offers an account of why regular rhythmic primes facilitate grammatical processing and why that effect is fragile, why musical experience transfers to speech, and why early insult can leave regularity extraction intact while productive language lags. We separate empirical findings from inferences and state five falsifiable predictions, spanning cross-species comparison, longitudinal development, clinical populations, intervention, and selective musical deficits.
articles.author: Tao Gong

articles.title: Vagus nerve stimulation in obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.content: BackgroundVagus nerve stimulation (VNS) has been investigated as a potential therapy for obesity because of the vagus nerve’s role in satiety, gastrointestinal signaling, autonomic regulation, and metabolic homeostasis. However, studies vary substantially in stimulation site, interface, parameters, species, diet condition, and reported outcomes.MethodsPubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception through May 6, 2026. Eligible studies evaluated chronic electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve or a defined vagal branch, included a comparator, and reported quantitative body weight data. Random-effects meta-analyses using Hedges’ g evaluated final body weight and weekly body weight change, while food intake, adiposity, metabolic outcomes, and safety were summarized narratively.ResultsOf 629 records identified, 23 publications met the inclusion criteria, yielding 25 experimental comparisons. Across 22 comparisons, VNS was associated with lower final body weight than control conditions (Hedges’ g = −1.07, 95% CI −1.43 to −0.72; I2 = 55.5%; P < 0.001). Across 14 comparisons, VNS was associated with lower weekly body weight gain or greater weekly body weight reduction (Hedges’ g = −2.82, 95% CI −4.23 to −1.41; I2 = 93.3%; P < 0.001). In animal studies, modality-specific final body weight estimates favored conventional implanted electrical VNS (g = −0.84), transcutaneous auricular VNS (g = −1.54), and self-powered triboelectric VNS (g = −8.36), although the triboelectric subgroup comprised two comparisons from one publication. Excluding the triboelectric comparisons, VNS remained associated with lower final body weight (g = −0.93, 95% CI −1.23 to −0.63, I2 = 39.4%). Food intake was commonly reduced after VNS, and adiposity outcomes generally favored stimulation, whereas metabolic and safety outcomes were reported inconsistently.ConclusionChronic, anatomically specific VNS was associated with lower body weight across predominantly preclinical studies. The final body weight estimate showed moderate heterogeneity, whereas the weekly body weight change estimate was highly heterogeneous and should be interpreted as supportive rather than as a precise estimate of effect magnitude. Translation to obesity treatment remains limited by sparse human evidence, potential small-study effects, and inconsistent reporting of metabolic and safety outcomes.

articles.title: Analysis and improvement of surface electromyography-based American Sign Language hand gesture recognition
articles.content: Surface electromyography (sEMG) allows sign language gestures to be recognized from forearm muscle activity without visual access to the hand. Gestures that produce similar forearm activation patterns, however, remain difficult to distinguish. This study examined how these similarities relate to classification errors and whether short-term temporal context improves recognition of static American Sign Language (ASL) gestures. We recorded 32-channel forearm sEMG from 10 participants performing 24 static gestures from the ASL alphabet and evaluated a dual-branch convolutional-Transformer classifier using both participant-specific and shared multi-user models. We also applied a Multi-Window Model that integrated the current and preceding window representations through causal attention after offline zero-phase filtering. On identical target windows, single-window classification achieved letter-only accuracies of 86.71% and 85.23% in the two settings, respectively. Nine low-recall letters formed three signal-similar groups, {A, M, N, S, T}, {E, O}, and {U, V}, with classification errors strongly concentrated within these groups. Spatial activation and independent-component analyses further showed that greater similarity in forearm sEMG patterns was associated with greater classification confusion. With the Multi-Window Model, letter-only accuracy increased to 90.77% in the participant-specific setting and 89.01% in the multi-user setting, with improvements observed across all participants in the participant-specific setting and larger gains for the nine low-recall letters. These findings demonstrate that integrating recent signal history can improve the accuracy of sEMG-based sign language gesture recognition, while persistent errors among highly similar gestures indicate an important limitation of the information available from forearm sEMG alone.
articles.author: Yasuharu Koike

articles.title: REFS: robust EEG feature selection with incomplete labels for multi-dimensional emotion recognition
articles.content: Objective. Compared to single-type features, multi-type electroencephalography (EEG) features provide a multi-level representation for analyzing multi-dimensional emotions. However, the high dimensionality of multi-type EEG features, combined with the relatively small number of high-quality EEG samples, poses challenges such as classifier overfitting and suboptimal real-time performance in the multi-dimensional emotion recognition task. As the number of EEG channels increases, the issue will become increasingly severe. Moreover, practical applications of affective brain–computer interface (a-BCI) frequently encounters partial absence of multi-dimensional emotional label data due to diverse emotional self-assessment models, and ambiguity and variability in individual emotion perception. Approach. To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel robust EEG feature selection method for incomplete multi-dimensional emotion recognition. The method leverages adaptive orthogonal latent semantic indexing to reconstruct the multi-dimensional emotional label space through second-order and higher-order relations, which could reduce the negative impact of missing values and outliers on label reconstruction. Simultaneously, it employs least squares regression with graph-based manifold learning regularization and global feature redundancy minimization regularization to enable EEG feature subset selection despite missing information, ultimately achieving robust and fast EEG-based multi-dimensional emotion recognition. Main results. The proposed method was validated on three multi-dimensional emotional datasets with varying channel configurations, namely DREAMER, DEAP and high-density EEG database, under different label missing ratios. Experimental results show that the proposed method consistently outperforms thirteen state-of-the-art feature selection methods in terms of robustness for EEG emotional feature selection across various missing ratios. Significance. The proposed method provides a robust and efficient solution for feature selection in multi-dimensional emotion recognition under incomplete EEG label scenarios, delivering reliable performance for practical a-BCI applications.
